falas.txt: This guy has trained for three years. Five days a week. He looks the part.

v.sub: 5 days a week. he LOOKS the part.

falas.txt: And his numbers have barely moved since year one.
He's not lazy. He works harder than almost anyone in the room.
The problem is five habits that feel like strength training, and aren't.

v.sub: that only FEEL like strength training

falas.txt: Here's where these habits come from.
Most gym advice was built by bodybuilders, for one goal. Bigger muscles.
And for that goal, a lot of it works.
But size and strength are two different targets. Related. Not the same.
You can train for years, hit one, and miss the other. That's what happened to our guy.

v.sub: that is what HAPPENED to him

falas.txt: Every one of them has been tested in a study. I'll show you each one.
And here's your job. Keep count of how many you do.
At the end, comment your score out of five. Most people who lift are at three or more. That's my guess, not a statistic.

v.sub: comment your SCORE at the end

falas.txt: Then I'll give you a one week fix for each.
None of these fixes need more time in the gym. Most of them need less effort, pointed in a better direction.

blocos.fonte: Schoenfeld et al. 2014 · J Strength Cond Res · 17 trained men · 8 weeks

falas.txt: Habit one. You live in the eight to twelve rep range.
Three sets of ten. On everything. For years.
It's what the poster on the wall says. It's what the machines are set up for. It's what everybody around you is doing.
It's not wrong. It builds muscle. But here's what it doesn't do.

v.sub: but here is what it does NOT do

falas.txt: Seventeen trained men were split into two groups. Same total work. Eight weeks.

num.rot: trained men · same total work · 8 weeks

falas.txt: One group did three sets of ten. The other did seven sets of three, with a much heavier bar.
Both groups built the same amount of muscle.
But the heavy group gained more strength on the bench press.
Same size. Different strength. Because lifting heavy is its own skill.
If you never touch a weight you can only lift three or four times, your body never learns to.

v.sub: so your body never LEARNS it

falas.txt: Heavy doesn't mean a one rep max every week. It means sets of three to five, where the bar moves well and you could do one more.

v.sub: and you could do ONE more

falas.txt: That's enough to teach your nervous system what heavy feels like.
If that's you, that's one.

blocos.fonte: Schoenfeld et al. 2016 · J Strength Cond Res · 21 trained men · 8 weeks

falas.txt: Habit two. You rest for one minute, because it feels more intense.
Heart pounding. Shirt soaked. Huge pump. It has to be working, right?
Twenty one trained men. Same program. One difference.
Half rested one minute between sets. Half rested three.
After eight weeks, the three minute group had gained more strength.
And here's the part that surprises people. More muscle, too.
The reason is simple. When you rush, your next set is weaker. Fewer reps, with less weight.
Being out of breath is not the same as getting stronger.

v.sub: is not the same as STRONGER

falas.txt: Short rests have a place. Conditioning. Small exercises at the end. Days when you have twenty minutes.
But on your main lift, the clock is not your friend. The bar is.

v.sub: is your friend. not the CLOCK.

falas.txt: If you watch the clock instead of the bar, that's two.

blocos.fonte: Davies et al. 2016 · Sports Medicine · 8 studies   |   Grgic et al. 2021 · J Sport Health Sci

falas.txt: Habit three. Every set goes to failure.
If you didn't collapse, it didn't count. That's the rule in a lot of gyms.
It feels like the most honest way to train. Nothing left in the tank.
Researchers pooled eight studies that compared the two ways to train.

num.rot: studies pooled · failure vs not to failure

falas.txt: Going to failure. And stopping a few reps short.
For strength, the results were about the same.
The authors' conclusion: failure isn't needed for strength. And if you use it, use it sparingly.
So what does failure cost you? Your next set. And sometimes your next workout.

v.sub: your next SET. your next workout.

falas.txt: Strength is practice. And you can't practice a clean heavy rep when you're wrecked.
A later analysis of more studies landed in the same place. Failure is not required, for strength or for size.
So keep failure for the last set of a small exercise. Curls. Raises. Not your squat.
If your last rep is always a fight for survival, that's three.

v.sub: if every set is a FIGHT

blocos.et: HABIT 4 · A NEW WORKOUT EVERY WEEK
blocos.fonte: Mattocks et al. 2017 · Med Sci Sports Exerc · 38 untrained adults · 8 weeks

falas.txt: Habit four. You change your exercises all the time.
New routine from a new video, every couple of weeks. To keep the muscle guessing.
And yes, I know. You might have found this channel that way. Stay with me.
Here's the problem. Strength is specific.
Thirty eight beginners. One group did hard sets, like a bodybuilder. The other group only practiced one thing: lifting a max.
Group one built more muscle. But both got equally strong at that lift.
A big part of strength is your nervous system learning one movement.

v.sub: one MOVEMENT. your nerves do that.

falas.txt: Change the movement every two weeks, and you restart the lesson every two weeks.
Variety isn't bad. Change your small exercises as often as you like.

v.sub: is fine for the SMALL stuff

falas.txt: But the two or three lifts you want to be strong at? Those need boredom. The good kind.
Pick a few lifts. Keep them for months. Let the numbers climb.
If you can't name your squat from eight weeks ago, that's four.

v.sub: if you cannot NAME your old numbers

blocos.et: HABIT 5 · STRAPS AND MACHINES FOR EVERYTHING
blocos.fonte: Winwood et al. 2015 · 30 trained rugby players · 7 weeks   |   Fain & Weatherford 2016 · 237 adults

falas.txt: Habit five. You outsource the hard parts.
Straps, so your grip never limits you. Machines, so nothing has to be balanced.
Both are useful tools. The habit is using them for everything.
Because your hands and your trunk are part of your strength. And they only grow when they're asked to work.
I'll be honest. The evidence here is thinner than for the other four.
But here's what we have. Young men today squeeze about twenty pounds less than young men did in nineteen eighty five.
And when thirty trained rugby players swapped barbell work for carries, logs, and sleds, for seven weeks,
they gained just as much as the barbell group.
Awkward, unsupported work counts. And a pad never taught anybody to brace.
Use straps on your heaviest set if your grip would cut it short. Just don't put them on for the warm up.

v.sub: straps there. not in the WARM UP.

falas.txt: If you can't remember your last set without straps, that's five.
So. What's your score?
Always eight to twelve. Racing the clock. Every set to failure. Always new exercises. Straps and machines.
Comment your number. No judgment. I'd bet the guy from the start of this video is a five.
And notice what all five have in common.
They all feel hard. Pump, sweat, burn, variety, exhaustion.
Your body doesn't get stronger from feeling tired. It gets stronger from lifting something heavy, well, again and again.
Tired is a side effect. It was never the goal.
And the opposite is true too. A great strength session can feel almost too easy. Long rests. Few reps. You leave fresh.
That feeling of, did I even work out? Get used to it. That's what practice feels like.

v.sub: that is what PRACTICE feels like

falas.txt: Here's the fix. You don't have to change your whole program.
One. Pick one big lift per workout. Do it first, heavy. Five sets of three.
Two. On that lift, rest three full minutes. Set a timer. It will feel lazy. Do it anyway.
Three. Stop every set with one or two good reps left.
Four. Keep the same main lifts for eight weeks, and write down every session.
Five. Finish with one carry. Heavy weights, no straps, walk until your grip is nearly gone.
Then do the rest of your workout exactly the way you like it. Tens, pumps, machines, all of it.
You're not giving anything up. You're adding the one thing that was missing.

v.sub: the one thing that was MISSING

falas.txt: Each week, add a little weight to that first lift. Five pounds is plenty. If the bar slows down a lot, hold the weight for another week.

v.sub: a week. or HOLD if it slows down.

falas.txt: Small, boring, written down. That's how the number moves.
And give it the full eight weeks before you judge it. Strength shows up slower than a pump, and it stays a lot longer.
This is a general starting point I put together, not a program from a study.
Heavy doesn't mean reckless. Learn the lift with a light bar first, and add weight slowly.
Use a spotter or safety bars for heavy sets. And if you have an injury, check with a professional first.
This is education, not medical advice.
So, back to the guy who's been stuck for two years.
He doesn't need more effort. He's already giving more than enough.
He needs to aim it. Heavier. Calmer. Fresher. The same lifts. And his own hands on the weight.
Eight weeks of that, and the numbers that haven't moved in years will move.
I can't promise how much. Nobody honest can. But the direction is not in doubt.
Comment your score out of five. And which habit you're fixing first.
And if you haven't done the three strength tests yet, that video is on the channel. Go get your numbers.
